title: Valid Parentheses
description:
# Valid Parentheses

Given a string `s` containing only the characters `'('`, `')'`, `'{'`, `'}'`, `'['`, and `']'`, determine whether `s` is a valid bracket string.

A bracket string is valid when all of these rules hold:

1. Every opening bracket is closed by the same bracket type.
2. Brackets close in the reverse order in which they were opened.
3. A closing bracket cannot appear unless it closes the most recent unmatched opening bracket.

The input contains no letters, digits, or spaces, so every character must participate in the bracket-matching rules.

## Example 1

**Input:** s = "()"
**Output:** true

## Example 2

**Input:** s = "()[]{}"
**Output:** true

## Example 3

**Input:** s = "(]"
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** The opening parenthesis cannot be closed by a square bracket.

## Example 4

**Input:** s = "([)]"
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** The square bracket opens after the parenthesis, so it must close before the parenthesis can close.

## Constraints

* `1 <= s.length <= 10^4`
* `s` consists only of the bracket characters `'()[]{}'`.

tests.description: Closing bracket type does not match the opener
Crossed nesting is invalid even though counts match
A closer cannot appear before any opener
Deep mixed nesting with adjacent groups
Valid prefix followed by an unmatched opener
Valid prefix followed by an extra closer
All three bracket types close in reverse order
Odd length and wrong closing order

solutions.name: Stack with Bracket Map
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan the string from left to right. Push opening brackets onto a stack. Store a map from each closing bracket to the opening bracket it requires, and when a closer appears, pop the stack and compare it with that required opener.

## Key Insight

The next valid closing bracket must close the most recent unmatched opener. A stack stores exactly that last-opened, first-closed order, while the map keeps type matching explicit.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Stack of Expected Closers
solutions.description:
## Approach

Instead of pushing the opening bracket, push the exact closing bracket that would be valid later. When a closing bracket is read, it must equal the value popped from the stack.

## Key Insight

This turns matching into a direct equality check. The stack no longer says what was opened; it says what the parser is waiting to see next, in the only order that can be valid.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Manual Array Stack
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a character array and a top pointer as the stack. Opening brackets are written into the array. A closing bracket pops one character and checks the exact matching type.

## Key Insight

This makes the stack abstraction concrete: a stack is just a buffer plus an index. It is useful for teaching what the library collection is doing internally.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Recursive Grammar Parser
solutions.description:
## Approach

Parse the string as a sequence of balanced bracket groups. When an opener appears, recursively parse everything until its matching closer. A closer is accepted only if it is exactly the closer expected by the current recursive frame.

## Key Insight

Valid bracket strings are a small grammar: a sequence can contain nested sequences, and each nested sequence has one required ending token. Recursion uses the call stack to represent those pending endings.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: String Reduction Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Repeatedly remove every adjacent valid pair: `()`, `[]`, and `{}`. If the string eventually becomes empty, every bracket was part of a properly nested pair; if no replacement changes the string, the remaining characters prove invalid structure.

## Key Insight

In a valid bracket string, the innermost pair is always adjacent. Removing all adjacent pairs preserves validity of the outer structure, so this baseline is a direct reduction proof even though it is slower.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
